How the scores are anchored

Accuracy conditions

Counts structural tests, not past hits. Asks whether the set-up would produce a good forecast at about five years.

  1. 5Passes 4–5 of the five tests, no known directional bias. A known, measurable bias costs one point at any level.
  2. 4Passes 3 tests, or 4–5 with a known, measurable bias.
  3. 3Passes 2 tests: accountable with a track record but no money at stake, or money at stake on a much shorter instrument.
  4. 2Passes 1 test: interested party, long-dated vendor roadmap, unscored panel or survey.
  5. 1Passes none: marketing, advocacy, unscored scenarios.
T1 Stakes the forecaster loses money, a licence or legal standing if wrong T2 Adversaries many informed parties set it, or someone is paid to attack it T3 Feedback marked regularly, with a published multi-year error record T4 Horizon fit the binding mechanism really reaches about five years T5 Pipeline the outcome is already largely in train: cohorts born, plants under construction, contracts signed

Worldbuilding richness

Can a writer lift dated, located, named events straight from it, or only extrapolate a line?

  1. 5Names entities, places, dates and quantities and explains its assumptions. Dozens of liftable facts.
  2. 4Disaggregated by sector, region or product with narrated drivers; some named specifics.
  3. 3Several series with brief commentary; few named specifics.
  4. 2A handful of headline series; minimal narrative.
  5. 1A single price or probability with no reasoning.

AI responsiveness

Has the latest edition actually moved its numbers for AI, or does it describe a world where nothing accelerates?

  1. 52026 edition and AI is a quantified, separately identified driver, or the instrument visibly re-prices on AI news.
  2. 42026 edition; AI analysed as a material driver with partial quantification.
  3. 32026 edition; AI acknowledged qualitatively but numbers unmoved, or a live price that embeds AI inseparably.
  4. 22025–26 edition with no AI treatment, or a method that structurally cannot respond. A 2025 edition that does treat AI is capped at 3.
  5. 1Latest edition pre-2025 with no AI treatment.

What the scoring shows

  • No type of source wins on all three scores. Market prices lead on accuracy conditions and trail on detail. Filings and enacted budgets are the reverse. Only 16 of 302 sources score 4 or more on every dimension, and most of them sit in energy and compute.
  • AI awareness follows money at stake, not institutional standing. 123 sources score 2 or below on AI. They include baselines usually treated as authoritative: the CMS health spending projections, the Social Security Trustees, NCES enrolment projections and the Survey of Professional Forecasters.
  • At five years, signed commitments beat liquid markets. Futures and prediction markets are deep for two or three years and thin after that. The sources that pass the horizon test are leases, power contracts, union contracts, statutes and capacity auctions, where a dated obligation already exists.
  • Bond markets did reprice in 2026. The ten-year real Treasury yield rose from 1.94% to 2.89% with inflation compensation steady near 2.2%, and the Fed's minutes name the AI build-out as a cause. Markets price an investment boom. They do not price a labour shock.
  • The compute build-out is documented mostly by its builders. Outside checks exist in a few places only: PJM's market monitor, regulators' staff cases that strip out uncontracted data-centre load, bond coupons and prediction markets. A scenario should lean on those where they disagree with the issuers.
  • The vocabulary changed mid-year. US federal documents dated after 29 September 2026 write “Super Intelligence (SI)” in place of AI, citing Executive Order 14434. Any text search of later filings needs both terms; the AI scores here were re-checked for it.

Money, prices & growth

26 sources scored · 5 shown · 40 of 49 primary documents downloaded in full

Official forecasts and bond prices now treat AI as an investment boom that pushes rates up, not as a jobs shock. The 10-year real yield rose from 1.94% to 2.89% during 2026 while the Fed's baseline keeps unemployment at 4.1% through 2029. A takeoff or mass-unemployment tail has a price only on Kalshi, and on thin volume.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Higher-for-longer interest rates The Fed is raising rates again (3.75-4.00% after a September 2026 hike, markets pricing a peak near 4.75% in 2027) and the 10-year Treasury is at 5.1%, so mortgages (rates the FOMC minutes call elevated), car loans, credit cards and business credit stay expensive well into the period.
  • Sticky inflation and cost of living PCE inflation is running 3.7% in 2026 on energy, tariffs and AI-related goods prices; the Fed staff does not see 2% until 2029, so real pay, rents and grocery and fuel bills are a live grievance for years.
  • Debt-financed AI investment boom AI capex is the main prop under growth and stock prices and is now financed with debt ($680bn issued Jan-Oct 2026); whether it keeps running or reverses decides jobs in construction and tech, retirement account values and credit availability.
  • Growth, jobs and recession risk Official baselines show 2-2.4% growth and 4.1% unemployment through 2029, while prediction markets put about 20-30% on a recession by 2027 and hiring is unusually slow; the gap between baseline and tail is what people will live through.
  • Public debt and term premium Federal debt is projected to rise from about 100% to 120% of GDP by 2036 (CBO February 2026 baseline as reported in secondary sources; primary not obtained) and investors are demanding a higher term premium, which raises every long-term borrowing rate and squeezes room for tax cuts or benefits.

AI & the compute build-out

24 sources scored · 5 shown · 97 of 119 primary documents downloaded in full

The richest and most AI-responsive material in the set: signed commitments broken out by year and counterparty, such as Alphabet's $924.4bn of purchase commitments running mostly through 2031. The weakness is shared authorship. Four of five picks are issuer documents, so the same optimism runs through all of them and the prediction markets are the only outside check.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Capital commitments: how many dollars and gigawatts are already contracted through ~2031 Trillions of dollars of signed purchase and lease commitments set how much AI capacity exists by 2028-2031, and therefore how cheap and ubiquitous AI services, agents and automation become at work and at home.
  • Chip, memory and packaging supply chain as the binding bottleneck (incl. export controls) Fabs, HBM memory and lithography tools ramp on multi-year schedules; shortages show up as rationed AI access, dearer phones/PCs/consoles and geopolitics around Taiwan and export licences.
  • Frontier-lab economics and AI capability trajectory (revenue run-rates, time horizons, AGI timing) How fast models improve and how much revenue labs earn decides which jobs are automated when, what software costs, and whether 'AGI announced' is a 2027 or a 2031 headline.
  • Financing structure and fragility: leases, guarantees, vendor finance, debt costs, bubble risk The build-out is financed with long leases, vendor guarantees and high-coupon debt; if revenue lags, the unwind hits pensions, bond funds, local tax bases and jobs, and if it holds, the same structures concentrate wealth.
  • Where it lands: gigawatt campuses, power, local siting fights and moratoria Gigawatt campuses land in specific counties (Ohio, Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee), bringing construction booms, gas turbines, grid strain, higher power bills and ballot fights over moratoria.

Energy & the grid

20 sources scored · 6 shown · 85 of 102 primary documents downloaded in full

The strongest area on all three scores at once. Forecasts are filed under regulatory challenge, itemised by zone and year, and treat data centres as a separate line. PJM has large-load demand rising from 11.5 GW in 2026 to 46.6 GW in 2031, and its capacity auction for 2028/29 cleared at the price cap, 6.8 GW short of the reliability requirement.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • AI data centres drive the first sustained US load growth in a generation Decides where campuses, substations and power lines appear (Northern Virginia, central Ohio, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana), which towns get construction booms, and whether new factories and homes wait in line for a grid connection.
  • Capacity scarcity and grid capex push household electricity bills up Capacity prices at the cap in PJM and multi-billion utility capex plans flow into monthly bills; regulators' fights over who pays (data centres vs households) become kitchen-table and election issues.
  • What gets built where: gas turbines, nuclear restarts/uprates, solar+storage, transmission Named plants with in-service dates (gas CCs for 2029-2033, restarted reactors, offshore wind, batteries) determine local jobs, air permits, land use fights and what the grid mix looks like by 2031.
  • Reliability margins thin: shortfalls against planning standards, large-load curtailment rules Auctions clearing thousands of MW short and NERC 'high risk' areas translate into conservation alerts, emergency orders keeping old coal plants open, and rules letting grid operators switch off data centres first.
  • Fuel-price shock and normalisation: 2026 Hormuz oil crisis, cheap US gas, LNG pull Brent above $100 in 2026 and a backwardated futures curve set petrol, diesel and heating costs; Henry Hub near $3-4 sets the marginal cost of US power and the profitability of the gas-plant build-out.

Work, wages & skills

26 sources scored · 5 shown · 99 of 120 primary documents downloaded in full

Official projections barely move for AI: the Fed holds unemployment flat and the BLS still adds 174,700 software developers by 2035. The AI signal is in documents where someone is committed, such as Block cutting from over 10,000 people to under 6,000 and a longshore contract that bars fully automated terminals until October 2030.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Occupational reshuffle: care, health and electricity-buildout jobs grow while office-admin, sales and routine clerical work shrinks Decides which jobs a 2030 household actually holds: who is a home-health aide, nurse practitioner or electrician, and whose receptionist, cashier, bookkeeping or call-centre job has quietly disappeared.
  • White-collar and entry-level hiring squeeze as large employers restructure around AI (flatter orgs, 'low-hire, low-fire') Graduates send hundreds of applications into flat hiring; mid-career managers and engineers see layers removed and headcount frozen even when their employer is growing.
  • Unbundling of labour-arbitrage industries: IT services, BPO/call centres and staffing pass AI productivity through to headcount and price Millions of jobs in Bengaluru, Manila and US call-centre towns depend on billing human hours; when clients demand AI savings, campus hiring and agent seats are the first to go.
  • Wage floors and bargained limits on automation: legislated minimum-wage steps and multi-year union contracts fix pay and technology rules to 2028-2030 Sets the pay packet and the pace of visible automation for low-wage workers, dockworkers, UPS drivers and Hollywood writers/actors, with dates already written into law or contract.
  • Slow labour-force growth and macro slack: ageing plus lower immigration mean tiny monthly payroll gains, ~4-4.6% baseline unemployment and a fat AI tail Determines whether work is easy or hard to find in a given year, how fast wages rise, and whether an AI shock arrives into a tight or a slack labour market.

Health, medicine & longevity

25 sources scored · 5 shown · 64 of 86 primary documents downloaded in full

Strong on dated prices and coverage rules, such as Wegovy's US list price falling to $675 on 1 January 2027 and Medicare paying $274 for semaglutide. Weak on AI: none of the actuarial baselines mentions it, and it appears only in company restructuring plans.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Cost of care outruns incomes Premiums, deductibles and Medicare Part B charges are set a year ahead and are rising 6–10% a year into 2027 (family employer premium $28,303 in 2026; ACA filings +15% median for 2027; per-capita spending $17,496 in 2026 to $22,095 in 2031), so health costs show up as smaller raises, bigger paycheck deductions and skipped care.
  • Coverage erosion and churn Expiry of enhanced ACA subsidies (2026) and Medicaid work/community-engagement rules (2027–28) push the uninsured from 28.6 million (2025) to about 33 million by 2028; insurers exit exchanges and trim Medicare Advantage, so people lose plans, doctors and continuity, and hospitals absorb uncompensated care.
  • GLP-1s, new drugs and government price-setting Obesity drugs become a mass consumer product (pills at $149–299 cash, $50 Medicare copay to end-2027, list price cut to $675 in 2027) while Medicare-negotiated prices arrive on fixed dates (2026, 2027, 2028) and next-generation drugs (retatrutide, CagriSema) reach approval – changing bodies, pharmacy counters and what a prescription costs.
  • Ageing, Medicare strain and slow longevity gains The last baby boomers turn 65 in 2029, Medicare enrollment passes 75 million by 2030, the hospital trust fund is projected to deplete in 2033, and official life-expectancy assumptions barely move – more retirees, higher premiums, crowded clinics and a looming benefit-cut debate.
  • AI and workforce strain in care delivery and administration AI is arriving first in billing, coding, prior authorisation and back offices (payers and pharma book AI-linked restructurings; employers blame AI-enabled billing for higher claims) and in 1,600+ FDA-authorised devices, against a clinician shortage – patients meet more software and fewer staff, and nobody in the official forecasts has priced it.

Housing, cities & local services

31 sources scored · 5 shown · 53 of 67 primary documents downloaded in full

City and transit budgets give the most liftable local detail in the set: New York's gaps of $6.2bn, $8.7bn and $9.0bn for fiscal 2028 to 2030, and MTA fare rises scheduled for March 2027 and March 2029. Almost none of it has absorbed AI. Loudoun County's budget leans on data-centre tax and never uses the term.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Mortgage rates near 7% and flat prices: the frozen, incentive-driven for-sale market Decides whether a household can buy, move or refinance: monthly payments, builder rate buydowns, lock-in keeping existing homes off the market, and whether home equity grows or stalls in real terms.
  • What gets built and what rent costs: the post-2025 multifamily supply drop, builder pipelines and state zoning mandates Sets rent renewals and vacancy in each metro, the number of new subdivisions and apartment towers opening near people, who is allowed to own rental houses, and how hard states push cities to permit homes.
  • City fiscal squeeze: structural budget gaps, pensions, federal aid cuts and what services survive Budget gaps turn into hiring freezes, shelter and rental-voucher limits, class sizes, library hours, tax and fee increases, and bond-rating fights that residents experience as service quality.
  • Transit and local capital programs: fare increases, deficits and dated megaproject schedules Commuters feel scheduled fare and toll increases, station closures for signal and accessibility work, new lines opening (or slipping), and whether trains are reliable enough to return to offices.
  • Office reset and the data-center tax base: who pays for local government, plus shrinking school enrollment Lease expirations and refinancing walls decide which downtown blocks empty or convert; data-center assessments let some counties cut car and home taxes while neighbours raise them; fewer children means school consolidations and closures.

Climate, insurance & physical risk

33 sources scored · 5 shown · 56 of 85 primary documents downloaded in full

Prices here are real and current but short: reinsurance resets yearly and catastrophe bonds run about three years. AI enters through contract wording, where insurers are now excluding it from general liability policies and selling separate cover.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Rising catastrophe losses vs. abundant reinsurance capital (soft cycle 2026-27, turn risk) Insured cat losses trend up 5-7% a year in real terms (USD 148bn trend for 2026, USD 186bn by 2030; modelled AAL USD 171bn) while record reinsurance and cat-bond capital is cutting rates 15-25%; the price of every property policy from 2027-31 depends on whether one USD 200-400bn peak year arrives and flips the cycle.
  • Home/auto insurance affordability and availability; residual markets and regulated rates Whether a household can buy home cover at all, and from whom: State Farm General +17% in California, FAIR Plan at 698,307 policies and USD 773bn exposure, Florida Citizens down to 278,246 policies at mid-2026 after mass takeouts, with rate cuts for most policyholders, national carriers not writing new homeowners in Florida, auto premiums now falling. Mortgages, home values and migration follow.
  • Insurers pricing or excluding AI and cyber risk From January 2026 standard liability forms can exclude anything 'arising out of generative artificial intelligence', and D&O carriers have absolute AI exclusions, while a small affirmative market (USD 15-25m limits) forms. Whether a business deploying AI agents is insured, and at what price, determines how fast AI is adopted and who pays when it fails; cyber rates are still falling.
  • Wildfire and climate liability shifting to utilities, ratepayers and public backstops Mega-fire losses are moving off insurers' books onto utility customers and state funds: Eaton Fire litigation (38,000 plaintiffs, bellwether trials in 2027), the California Wildfire Fund, customer-funded self-insurance collected through electric rates, NFIP on serial short-term extensions, TWIA cutting required funding from 1-in-100 to 1-in-50. Shows up in power bills, surcharges and assessments.
  • Carbon prices and the warming trajectory (policy and physical baseline) EU allowances trade around EUR 85/t with ETS2 on heating and road fuel due in 2028; California allowances clear near USD 32; pledges imply ~2.6C. A strong 2026-27 El Nino has markets pricing 2026 as the hottest year on record at ~92%. These set fuel, heating and food prices and the physical baseline the insurers above are pricing.

Public finances & what government delivers

27 sources scored · 5 shown · 62 of 80 primary documents downloaded in full

The February 2026 CBO baseline has already been overtaken. It assumed a 4.1% ten-year Treasury rate for 2026 and the market stood at 5.10% on 17 November. Enacted statutes are the reliable part: they give exact dates for benefit rules, tax changes and AI compliance duties.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • Federal debt-service squeeze: ~6%-of-GDP deficits, interest above defense, higher long rates Interest on the debt already exceeds defence and is the fastest-growing federal outlay; 10-year Treasuries above 5% (Nov 2026) feed straight into mortgage, car-loan and business rates and leave less room for everything else government does.
  • Entitlement cliffs and benefit retrenchment (Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP, ACA) Dated cliffs and rule changes hit households directly: Medicaid work rules from 1 Jan 2027, SNAP costs shifted to states from FY2028, lapsed ACA subsidies, Highway Trust Fund exhaustion in 2028, and the 2032-33 Social Security and Medicare hospital-fund depletion dates that dominate late-decade politics.
  • Tax and tariff regime churn: OBBBA sunsets, court-voided tariffs, refunds, yearly IRS resets Take-home pay and prices move with law: tip, overtime and senior deductions expire after 2028, tariffs were voided by the Supreme Court and re-imposed under other statutes, importers chase refunds, and brackets reset each November.
  • State and local budget stress and federal cost-shifting (deficits, pensions, service cuts) States must balance budgets while absorbing federal cost-shifts: California's structural gap (about $35bn a year from 2027-28 on the LAO's November 2025 numbers), New York out-year gaps and pension contributions translate into tuition, transit, school and clinic decisions people see locally.
  • Government adoption and regulation of AI on binding timetables Whether a benefit claim, job application or loan is decided by software, and what notice and appeal a person gets, is being fixed by statutes with start dates (Colorado 1 Jan 2027; EU 2 Dec 2027 and 2 Aug 2028) while Washington buys AI tools government-wide and sues to pre-empt state rules.

Geopolitics, security & politics

33 sources scored · 5 shown · 62 of 103 primary documents downloaded in full

Budgets and order backlogs fix the defence build-up in dollars and delivery years: Lockheed Martin's backlog stood at $292.0bn in September 2026 and the administration's plan lifts base defence from $1.15tn in 2027 to $1.36tn in 2031. Markets cover politics only to about 2028 or 2029. Polymarket puts a Chinese invasion of Taiwan by the end of 2027 at 8.5%.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • US-China rivalry: Taiwan risk and the AI-chip/compute control regime Determines whether the Taiwan Strait stays open (chips, shipping, markets), which countries can buy or rent frontier AI compute, and how much of consumer electronics and cloud capacity is priced with a security premium.
  • Rearmament super-cycle: US $1.5T budgets, NATO 3.5%/5%, munitions, ships and autonomy at scale Defence is becoming a top-three budget line across the West: it sets taxes and borrowing, pulls skilled labour into shipyards, missile and drone plants, reshapes regional job markets (Ohio, Barrow, Unterluess, Newport News) and normalises conscription and civil-defence debates.
  • Hot wars and their settlement: Russia-Ukraine, Iran/Hormuz, with shipping and energy spillovers Ceasefire-or-escalation outcomes in Ukraine and the Gulf drive fuel and food prices, insurance and freight costs, refugee flows, and whether European and Gulf cities live under drone and missile alert regimes.
  • Political control and legitimacy: the 2027-2030 election cycle and leadership transitions Who holds the US presidency and Congress after 2028, the French presidency after 2027, and how Xi and Putin handle 2027 and 2030 milestones decides the rule-of-law climate, alliance credibility and the direction of AI, trade and migration policy people actually live under.
  • Trade-regime fragmentation: tariffs by rotating statute, USMCA limbo, state-directed industrial policy Tariffs imposed, struck down and re-imposed under different statutes change shelf prices and supply chains quarter by quarter; an un-renewed USMCA and Section 232 actions put North American car, steel and chip jobs under a standing question mark.

People: population, migration, ageing & education

25 sources scored · 5 shown · 67 of 85 primary documents downloaded in full

The most predetermined area and the least AI-aware. Cohort sizes for 2031 are fixed by births that have already happened, so migration is the open variable, and the Census Bureau's 2023 projection assumed 865,000 net migrants in 2026 against about 321,000 in its current estimate. Education-company filings are the one place AI is quantified.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • US immigration reversal and enforcement build-out Decides who is available to build houses, staff care homes, pick crops and fill classrooms: official assumptions cut non-LPR inflows for 2026–2030 by roughly 30–45%, $75bn of detention and ICE money runs to 2029, skilled-visa and refugee channels are nearly closed.
  • Falling births and near-zero natural population growth Fewer babies each year (3.61m in 2025) empties maternity wards, day-care and kindergartens first; deaths are projected to exceed births around 2030, so any local growth depends on migration.
  • Ageing: the 80+ boom, care demand and pension strain About 7.7 million more Americans aged 65+ by 2030 and the 80+ group up roughly 28%: families hunt for care places as occupancy and prices rise, and the retirement trust fund hits its depletion date in 2032.
  • Enrolment cliff: shrinking school and college cohorts, closures, fewer international students The US graduating class peaked in 2025 and shrinks unevenly (Illinois minus 14% by 2030); districts close schools, small colleges merge or close, and foreign students who paid full price are down 15% among new enrolments.
  • AI rewiring how students learn and what education businesses survive Half of teens already use chatbots for schoolwork; homework-help firms are collapsing, computer-science majors are falling 12% a year and PISA scores are at record lows — what school is for, and which credentials pay, is being renegotiated.

Mobility, robots & everyday technology

32 sources scored · 5 shown · 56 of 83 primary documents downloaded in full

Filings carry hard dates, such as the first 777-9 delivery in 2027 and Starlink at 13.6 million consumer subscribers. This area also has the widest gap between issuer targets and outside forecasts, so prediction markets do the most work here.

Trends these sources need to cover
  • robotaxis: driverless ride-hailing goes from a few metros to an ordinary urban service Waymo alone logged about 1.5 million paid driverless trips a month in California by Sept 2026; whether your city has cars with no driver (and what that does to fares, drivers and parking) is one of the most visible changes of 2026-31.
  • ev-transition: the car market splits by region (China majority-electric, Europe rule-driven, US stalled after credits ended) Determines what is in showrooms, what a commute costs, where chargers appear and which factories open or are written off.
  • robots-drones: robots leave the lab - record factory installs, first humanoid production lines, drone delivery waiting on the BVLOS rule Changes who (or what) works in warehouses and plants, and whether parcels and take-away arrive by air in suburbs.
  • air-travel-and-space: flying is capped by aircraft supply while launch cadence and air taxis are the wildcards A decade-long jet backlog and slow rate ramps mean older planes and firm fares into the 2030s; eVTOL and supersonic remain marginal; rockets fly more than a hundred times a year.
  • connectivity-devices-agents: ambient connectivity and AI-first devices - satellite broadband and direct-to-phone, 6G around 2030, AI glasses, pricier phones, agents that shop and pay Coverage dead zones close, the main screen starts to move from phone to wearables and assistants, and checkout increasingly happens through an agent.

Method and limits

  • Each area was researched separately, then every score was re-read against the anchors and adjusted so that a 4 means the same thing in every area.
  • Top picks are the highest combined scores in an area, subject to covering different trends and mechanisms. Near-duplicates were held back to the longer list.
  • A document counts as downloaded in full only if the complete official file is on disk and opens. Text captures, summaries and single volumes of a set count as partial. All files, 1.95 GB and 17,619 pages of them, are in the repository under scenario-sources/primary/, indexed in manifest.json.
  • Every quote was checked by script against the text of the downloaded file. The check ignores spacing and punctuation but requires the exact word sequence. Quotes that failed were removed, not edited.
  • Accuracy conditions describe incentives and structure. They are not a measured hit rate, and plans made under strong incentives still slip: capacity plans run late and utilities have a record of over-forecasting load.
  • The source set leans to the United States because that is where filings are most detailed and most public.
